Into the Unknown: Deep Dive into the Linux Network Stack

Introduction

Most people know Linux as a server operating system. This workshop shows Linux as a network platform: a router, a switch, an EVPN leaf or a BGP speaker that fits into the network around it. In the labs you build the data plane by hand, look at how the kernel (and the user-space data planes that replace it) forwards packets, and connect it to a standard routing control plane.

Every lab is a small network built with containerlab. Each node is a container, and the links between nodes are virtual Ethernet links. You deploy the lab with one command, do the exercises, and destroy it at the end.

Labs overview

Lab Title Summary
1 Native kernel features (VRF / NETNS / VETH / MPLS) You add a plain Linux host to an MPLS L3VPN network using only iproute2: network namespaces, veth pairs, a VRF, a TAP interface and static MPLS routes. The host then pushes its own MPLS label stack into the core.
2 Linux as an EVPN/VXLAN leaf You turn a Linux host into an EVPN/VXLAN leaf with a VRF, Linux bridges and VXLAN interfaces (L2 and L3 VNIs). FRR provides the BGP EVPN control plane.
3 Alternative DP – OVS/OVN You build the same tenant network as in LAB 2 with OVN on top of Open vSwitch, configured from one central place. OVN also provides routing and DHCP.
4 DPDK & VPP You connect three routers that use VPP as the data plane and FRR as the control plane, with memif, vhost-user and DPDK virtio_user links. The VPP linux-cp plugin syncs addresses and routes from Linux into VPP.
5 VRRP + GoBGP & Bird Two web servers share one service IP. keepalived (VRRP) picks the active server, GoBGP advertises the IP only from that server, and a BIRD route reflector changes route attributes based on BGP communities.

The labs are fully independent. No lab uses the results of another lab. If you skip a lab or do not finish it, the next labs still work.

Requirements

  • A dedicated VM. Each participant gets their own virtual machine with SSH access. Everything the labs need (containerlab, Docker, container images, lab files) is already installed on it.

  • Login details. Your login, password and the VM's domain name are given to you before the first lab.

  • An SSH client on your laptop:

    • Linux / macOS: the built-in ssh command in a terminal.
    • Windows: the built-in OpenSSH client (ssh in PowerShell or Windows Terminal), or a client such as PuTTY.
    ssh <login>@<vm-domain-name>

  • No file editing on the VM. You type all commands yourself in the terminal. You do not need to edit any files on the VM, so you do not need a remote editor.

Running a lab

Each lab is in its own directory (lab1 … lab5) in your home directory on the VM. The basic flow is the same for every lab:

cd lab1
containerlab deploy -t lab1.clab.yml     # build the lab
containerlab inspect -t lab1.clab.yml    # list nodes and management IPs
# ... exercises ...
containerlab destroy -t lab1.clab.yml    # remove the lab

All labs uses the same management network (172.16.0.0/24). Destroy the current lab before you deploy the next one.

Accessing the nodes: docker exec instead of SSH

Every node in a lab has an SSH server, and the root key is already installed, so ssh root@<management-ip> or ssh root@<node-name> works. In the labs we use docker exec instead, because it is faster and simpler. Example:

docker exec -it <node> sh        # e.g. docker exec -it ppe sh

What this command does:

  • docker exec starts a new process inside a running container (emulating a device). Here the process is a shell (sh or bash).
  • -i keeps the input open and -t allocates a terminal, so you get a normal interactive shell.
  • The shell runs in the container's namespaces, so it sees the container's network interfaces, routing tables and processes, the same as a session opened with SSH.

How it differs from SSH:

docker exec ssh root@<ip>
Path Local call to the Docker engine on the VM TCP connection to the SSH server in the node, over the management network
Target Container name Management IP address
Authentication None (you already have access to Docker) Root key
Needs network and an SSH server in the node No Yes

For the labs there is no difference. In both cases you get a root shell in the node and see exactly the same network state.

To leave the node's shell, type exit or press Ctrl+D.

If something goes wrong

  1. Rebuild the lab. You can always destroy the lab and deploy it again. This gives you a clean lab in its start state:

    containerlab destroy -t labN.clab.yml
containerlab deploy -t labN.clab.yml

  2. Restore from backup. If the step above does not help (for example, lab files were deleted or changed), run the recovery script. It restores all labs from a backup:

    /usr/local/bin/recover_labs.sh

Getting help

If you have a question or get stuck, do not hesitate to call the instructor.

There is also a Slack channel for this workshop: #ac6-ws-a3-into-the-unknown. If you do not have access to that Slack workspace yet, join with this invitation link:

https://join.slack.com/t/networkautomationfrm/shared_invite/zt-4c0zlio86-l~zhtYRJP8f6UTM_GLkPdA

Follow the steps of each lab precisely but most importantly - HAVE FUN!

LAB 1 – Native kernel features (VRF / NETNS / VETH / MPLS)

Goals

In this lab you will build part of the data plane by hand, using only iproute2 commands. After this lab you should be able to:

  • explain how containers map to Linux network namespaces (netns),
  • connect two namespaces with a veth pair,
  • create a Linux VRF and attach interfaces to it,
  • create a TAP interface and inject packets into the kernel through it,
  • read and modify the IPv4 and MPLS routing tables (static routes, MPLS push / pop),
  • check the OSPF / LDP / BGP (L3VPN) control plane run by FRR.

Topology

Node Role Interface Address Notes
CE1 Customer router, AS65001 eth1 192.168.1.2/30 lo: 192.168.100.1/24
PE1 PE router, AS64512 eth1 10.1.0.2/30 lo: 100.65.0.1/32
eth2 192.168.1.1/30 in VRF LAB1 (table 101)
PPE P router + BGP RR eth1 10.1.0.1/30 lo: 100.65.0.100/32
eth2 10.2.0.1/30
veth3 10.3.0.1/30 created in this lab
PE2 PE router, AS64512 eth1 10.2.0.2/30 lo: 100.65.0.2/32
eth2 192.168.2.1/30 in VRF LAB1 (table 101)
CE2 Customer router, AS65002 eth1 192.168.2.2/30 lo: 192.168.200.1/24
LAB Plain Linux host veth1 10.3.0.2/30 created in this lab
tap0 192.168.3.1/24 in VRF LAB1 (table 101)

Management addresses (network 172.16.0.0/24): PPE .10, PE1 .11, PE2 .12, LAB .13, CE1 .21, CE2 .22.

What is already configured when the lab starts:

  • FRR on CE1, PE1, PPE, PE2 and CE2 (OSPF + LDP in the core, iBGP VPNv4 with PPE as the route reflector, eBGP between PE and CE inside VRF LAB1).
  • VRF LAB1 on PE1 and PE2.
  • On PE1, a static MPLS route: label 1000 → pop and look up in VRF LAB1.

Your job is to add the LAB node to this network. LAB acts like a very simple PE: it sends traffic from its own VRF, with an MPLS label stack it pushes itself, over a veth link into the MPLS core.

Deploying the lab and accessing nodes

Go to the lab directory, deploy the lab and list its nodes:

cd lab1
containerlab deploy -t lab1.clab.yml
containerlab inspect -t lab1.clab.yml

containerlab inspect lists six nodes (ce1, ce2, lab, pe1, pe2, ppe) in state running, with their management IP addresses.

To open a shell on a node:

docker exec -it <node> sh        # e.g. docker exec -it ppe sh
# or
ssh root@172.16.0.10             # PPE via its management IP

To open the FRR CLI on a router node (CE1, CE2, PE1, PE2, PPE):

docker exec -it pe1 vtysh

Tip: In Task 4 you will need several terminals open at the same time.

Note: Do not run ./setup.sh or /tmp/setup.sh. Those scripts are the reference solution. In this lab you type every command yourself.

Task 0 – Check the existing control plane

Before you change anything, make sure the core works.

0.1 OSPF and LDP (on PPE) [ optional ]

Check the OSPF neighbors, the LDP sessions and the LDP label bindings on PPE:

docker exec -it ppe vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec -it ppe vtysh -c "show mpls ldp neighbor"
docker exec -it ppe vtysh -c "show mpls ldp binding"

Expected result: PPE has two OSPF neighbors (100.65.0.1 and 100.65.0.2) in state Full, and two LDP sessions in state OPERATIONAL.

0.2 MPLS forwarding table in the kernel [ optional ]

FRR (zebra) programs the LDP labels into the kernel. Check them with iproute2:

docker exec -it ppe ip -f mpls route show
docker exec -it pe1 ip -f mpls route show

On PE1 you should also see the static route that was added at deploy time:

1000 dev LAB1

0.3 VRF on PE1 [ optional ]

Look at VRF LAB1 on PE1: its routing table, its interfaces and its routes:

docker exec -it pe1 ip vrf show
docker exec -it pe1 ip -d link show LAB1
docker exec -it pe1 ip link show master LAB1
docker exec -it pe1 ip route show vrf LAB1

Expected result: VRF LAB1 uses table 101. eth2 is enslaved to it. The VRF table has the CE1 prefix 192.168.100.0/24 (learned by eBGP) and the CE2 prefix 192.168.200.0/24 (learned over the L3VPN, with an MPLS encap).

0.4 BGP / L3VPN [ optional ]

Check the iBGP sessions on the route reflector (PPE), the VPNv4 routes and the VRF routes on PE1, and the BGP routes that CE1 receives:

docker exec -it ppe vtysh -c "show bgp summary"
docker exec -it pe1 vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 vpn"
docker exec -it pe1 vtysh -c "show bgp vrf LAB1 ipv4 unicast"
docker exec -it ce1 vtysh -c "show ip route bgp"

Expected result: PPE has two iBGP neighbors (100.65.0.1 and 100.65.0.2), each with 2 received prefixes. PE1 has the VPNv4 routes of both sites (Route Distinguishers 100.65.0.1:101 and 100.65.0.2:101), and VRF LAB1 on PE1 has 192.168.100.0/24 and 192.168.200.0/24. CE1 has a BGP route to 192.168.200.0/24 via 192.168.1.1 (PE1).

0.5 End-to-end check CE1 ↔ CE2

Ping the CE2 loopback from the CE1 loopback:

docker exec -it ce1 ping -c 3 -I 192.168.100.1 192.168.200.1

The ping must work. This traffic goes CE1 → PE1 (VRF) → MPLS core → PE2 (VRF) → CE2.

Task 1 – Connect PPE and LAB with a veth pair (on the host)

Every container has its own network namespace. Containerlab registers these namespaces under /var/run/netns, using the node names. This means you can manage them from the host with ip netns and ip -n <netns>.

1.1 List the namespaces

List the network namespaces on the host:

sudo ip netns list
ls -l /var/run/netns/

You should see ppe, pe1, pe2, ce1, ce2 and lab.

1.2 Create the veth pair

A veth pair is a virtual cable: whatever goes into one end comes out of the other end. Create the pair in the host namespace:

sudo ip link add veth3 type veth peer veth1
ip link show type veth | grep -E 'veth1|veth3'

You should see two interfaces, veth1@veth3 and veth3@veth1, both in state DOWN. The name after @ is the other end of the pair.

1.3 Move each end into its namespace

Move veth3 into the PPE namespace and veth1 into the LAB namespace:

sudo ip link set veth3 netns ppe
sudo ip link set veth1 netns lab

The commands print nothing when they succeed.

1.4 Verify

Check that each end is now in its namespace and not on the host:

ip link show veth3                         # error: the device is not in the host netns any more
sudo ip -n ppe link show veth3             # veth3@if<N> in PPE
sudo ip -n lab link show veth1             # veth1@if<N> in LAB

-n executes command in netns.

Task 2 – Configure PPE

Open a shell on PPE:

docker exec -it ppe bash

2.1 Let FRR configure veth3

The FRR config of PPE already contains a section for veth3 (10.3.0.1/30, passive OSPF, mpls enable). The interface did not exist when FRR started, so reload FRR to apply this config:

sv reload /services/frr

Verify (wait a few seconds):

ip addr show veth3                          # 10.3.0.1/30 must be present
sysctl net.mpls.conf.veth3.input            # must be 1, so the kernel accepts MPLS on veth3
vtysh -c "show interface veth3"
vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"            # OSPF and LDP must come back in Full state

mpls enable in FRR sets net.mpls.conf.<if>.input=1. Without this setting, the kernel drops every MPLS packet that arrives on the interface.

2.2 Add a static MPLS "pop" route

LAB will send packets with the label stack 1000/1000. PPE must remove (pop) the top label and send the packet to PE1 (10.1.0.2) through eth1. The inner label 1000 stays on the packet:

ip -f mpls route add 1000 via inet 10.1.0.2 dev eth1

Verify:

ip -f mpls route show
ip -f mpls route get 1000

Expected entry:

1000 via inet 10.1.0.2 dev eth1

There is no as <label> in this route. This means pop: the kernel does not push a new label. Compare it with the LDP routes in the same table, which use as to <label> (swap).

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

Task 3 – Configure LAB

Open a shell on LAB:

docker exec -it lab bash

3.1 Configure the veth1 interface

Give veth1 its address and bring it up:

ip addr add 10.3.0.2/30 dev veth1
ip link set veth1 up

Verify:

ip addr show veth1           # state UP, 10.3.0.2/30
ping -c 3 10.3.0.1           # PPE must reply

3.2 Create the VRF

Create VRF LAB1 with routing table 101 and bring it up:

ip link add LAB1 type vrf table 101
ip link set LAB1 up

Verify:

ip vrf show
ip -d link show LAB1

ip vrf show lists LAB1 with table 101, and ip -d link show LAB1 shows vrf table 101.

3.3 Add a route that pushes two MPLS labels

This route goes into the VRF table (101). It pushes two labels: the outer label is for PPE, and the inner label is the "VPN label" for PE1. This way LAB works like a PE router:

ip route add table 101 192.168.100.0/24 encap mpls 1000/1000 via 10.3.0.1 dev veth1

ip route add vrf LAB1 ... does the same thing as table 101.

Verify:

ip route show vrf LAB1
ip route show table 101

Expected entry:

192.168.100.0/24  encap mpls  1000/1000 via 10.3.0.1 dev veth1

3.4 Create the TAP interface

A TAP device is a virtual Ethernet interface. A user-space program controls the other end: every frame that the program writes to /dev/net/tun shows up in the kernel as a frame received on tap0.

ip tuntap add dev tap0 mode tap
ip link set tap0 addr 02:00:00:00:00:02

The test script sends frames with destination MAC 02:00:00:00:00:02. This is why we set the MAC of tap0 to that value. Otherwise the kernel would treat the frames as "not for me" and drop them.

3.5 Put tap0 in the VRF and assign an IP address

Attach tap0 to VRF LAB1, give it an address and bring it up:

ip link set tap0 master LAB1
ip addr add 192.168.3.1/24 dev tap0
ip link set tap0 up

Verify:

ip link show master LAB1         # tap0 must be listed
ip -d link show tap0             # "tun type tap", MAC 02:00:00:00:00:02
ip addr show tap0
ip route show vrf LAB1           # connected 192.168.3.0/24 + MPLS route to 192.168.100.0/24

tap0 shows NO-CARRIER / state DOWN until a program opens it. This is normal.

3.6 Check IP forwarding

The kernel must forward packets from tap0 to veth1:

sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward       # must be 1

If it is 0, enable it with sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1.

Exit the device/docker shell using: exit

Task 4 – Send traffic and follow it hop by hop

The script /tmp/send_tap.py on LAB opens tap0 and writes one Ethernet frame to it:

Ether 02:00:00:00:00:01 -> 02:00:00:00:00:02
IP    192.168.3.99      -> 192.168.100.100
ICMP  echo request

4.1 Start the captures (one terminal per command)

Start tcpdump at four points along the path, each in its own terminal:

# Terminal 1 – PPE, link from LAB (expect 2 labels)
docker exec -it ppe tcpdump -nei veth3 mpls

# Terminal 2 – PPE, link to PE1 (expect 1 label)
docker exec -it ppe tcpdump -nei eth1 mpls

4.1.1 Start the additional captures [ optional ]

# Terminal 3 – PE1, core link (expect 1 label)
docker exec -it pe1 tcpdump -nei eth1 mpls

# Terminal 4 – PE1, link to CE1 (expect plain IP/ICMP)
docker exec -it pe1 tcpdump -nei eth2 icmp

4.2 Send the packet

In a fifth terminal, send one test frame from LAB:

docker exec -it lab /tmp/send_tap.py

Output: Sent 42 bytes to tap0. Run it a few times if needed.

4.3 Expected results

Capture point What you should see
PPE veth3 MPLS (label 1000 ...) (label 1000 ..., [S] ...) IP 192.168.3.99 > 192.168.100.100: ICMP echo request
PPE eth1 MPLS (label 1000, ..., [S] ...) IP 192.168.3.99 > 192.168.100.100: ICMP echo request (outer label popped)
PE1 eth1 Same as PPE eth1
PE1 eth2 IP 192.168.3.99 > 192.168.100.100: ICMP echo request (no labels, sent to CE1)

[S] marks the bottom of the label stack. Also check the MPLS TTL at each hop.

CE1 has no route back to 192.168.3.0/24, so no echo reply is expected. The goal is to follow the request through the network.

4.4 Packet walk – what happened?

  1. LAB: send_tap.py writes the frame to tap0. The kernel receives it on tap0. tap0 is in VRF LAB1, so the kernel looks up the route in table 101. The route for 192.168.100.0/24 pushes the labels 1000/1000 and sends the packet out of veth1 to 10.3.0.1.
  2. veth pair: the frame leaves veth1 (netns lab) and arrives on veth3 (netns ppe).
  3. PPE: MPLS input is enabled on veth3. The kernel looks up label 1000 in the MPLS table. The rule is: pop, then send to 10.1.0.2 via eth1. The packet leaves with one label (1000).
  4. PE1: MPLS input is enabled on eth1 (FRR mpls enable). The kernel looks up label 1000: pop and deliver to device LAB1. This means another IP lookup, this time in VRF LAB1 (table 101).
  5. PE1 VRF LAB1: 192.168.100.0/24 was learned from CE1 over eBGP. The packet leaves eth2 as plain IP.

Troubleshooting checklist

Symptom Check
Nothing on PPE veth3 LAB: ip route show vrf LAB1, ip link show master LAB1, MAC of tap0, sysctl net.ipv4.ip_forward
Packets on veth3 but not on eth1 PPE: sysctl net.mpls.conf.veth3.input, ip -f mpls route show
Packets on PE1 eth1 but not on eth2 PE1: ip -f mpls route show (route 1000 dev LAB1), ip route show vrf LAB1
encap mpls route is rejected Host: lsmod | grep mpls – modules mpls_router and mpls_iptunnel must be loaded
veth3 has no IP address PPE: restart FRR again (sv restart /services/frr)

Look at kernel drop counters with ip -s link show <if>.

Cleanup

containerlab destroy -t lab1.clab.yml

The veth pair is deleted automatically when the ppe and lab namespaces are removed.

LAB 2 – Linux as an EVPN/VXLAN leaf

Goals

In this lab you turn a Linux host (BMS1) into an EVPN/VXLAN leaf. You build the data plane by hand with iproute2, and FRR provides the EVPN control plane. After this lab you should be able to:

  • use a Linux VRF as the tenant routing table of an EVPN leaf,
  • build Linux bridges that act as L2 segments and as gateways (SVIs),
  • create VXLAN interfaces and attach them to bridges as L2 VNIs (bridging) and as an L3 VNI (routing between leaves),
  • see how a VLAN-aware bridge (BMS2, BMS-DHCP) does the same job with one bridge,
  • connect all of this to FRR (BGP EVPN), and check the result in FRR and in the kernel.

Topology

Tenant networks (VRF LAB2, table 101)

Network Subnet Gateway (anycast) VLAN (BMS2/BMS-DHCP) VNI Present on
red 192.168.1.0/24 192.168.1.1 100 100 BMS1, BMS2, BMS-DHCP
green 192.168.2.0/24 192.168.2.1 200 200 BMS1, BMS2, BMS-DHCP
orange 192.168.3.0/24 192.168.3.1 300 300 BMS-DHCP only
L3 VNI – – 1000 1000 BMS1, BMS2, BMS-DHCP

Hosts

Node Address Connected to Notes
vm1-red DHCP (red) BMS1 vtap0 gets its lease from dhcp-red
vm1-green DHCP (green) BMS1 vtap1 gets its lease from dhcp-green
vm2-red 192.168.1.202/24 BMS2 vtap0 static
vm2-green 192.168.2.202/24 BMS2 vtap1 static
dhcp-red 192.168.1.200/24 BMS-DHCP vtap0 dnsmasq, pool 192.168.1.10–100
dhcp-green 192.168.2.200/24 BMS-DHCP vtap1 dnsmasq, pool 192.168.2.10–100
www 192.168.3.200/24 BMS-DHCP vtap2 web server

Management addresses (network 172.16.0.0/24): BMS1 .11, BMS2 .12, BMS-DHCP .13, vm1-red .21, vm1-green .22, vm2-red .23, vm2-green .24, dhcp-red .31, dhcp-green .32, www .33, l2-switch .40.

Control plane (FRR)

  • Underlay: eBGP IPv4 unicast over 10.1.0.0/24. BMS1 (AS 65001) and BMS2 (AS 65002) peer with BMS-DHCP (AS 65100) and advertise their loopbacks. The route-map ZEBRA-SRC sets each loopback as the source address for these routes, so VXLAN packets leave with the loopback (VTEP) address as source.
  • Overlay: iBGP AS 64512, address family l2vpn evpn, between loopbacks. BMS-DHCP is the route reflector.
  • vrf LAB2 / vni 1000: VRF LAB2 uses VNI 1000 as its L3 VNI. advertise ipv4 unicast: the VRF's connected subnets are advertised as EVPN type-5 (prefix) routes.

What is already configured when the lab starts:

  • FRR on BMS1, BMS2 and BMS-DHCP (the config above).
  • The full data plane on BMS2 and BMS-DHCP, using one VLAN-aware bridge br0.
  • Static addresses on vm2-, dhcp- and www. The DHCP servers are running.

Your job is to build the data plane on BMS1. To keep it simple you do not use VLANs on BMS1. Instead, you create a separate bridge for each network.

Deploying the lab and accessing nodes

Go to the lab directory, deploy the lab and list its nodes:

cd lab2
containerlab deploy -t lab2.clab.yml
containerlab inspect -t lab2.clab.yml

containerlab inspect lists eleven nodes in state running, with their management IP addresses.

To open a shell on a node:

docker exec -it <node> sh        # e.g. docker exec -it bms1 sh
# or
ssh root@172.16.0.11             # BMS1 via its management IP

To open the FRR CLI on BMS1, BMS2 or BMS-DHCP:

docker exec -it bms1 vtysh

Note: Do not run ./setup.sh or /tmp/setup.sh. Those scripts are the reference solution. In this lab you type every command yourself.

Task 0 – Check the starting point

0.1 Underlay on BMS1

Check the BGP sessions and the kernel routes on BMS1, then ping the BMS2 loopback from the BMS1 loopback:

docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 unicast summary"
docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn summary"
docker exec -it bms1 ip route
docker exec -it bms1 ping -c 3 -I 100.65.0.101 100.65.0.102

Expected result:

  • The eBGP session to 10.1.0.1 is Established.
  • The iBGP EVPN session to 100.65.0.1 is Established.
  • The kernel has routes to 100.65.0.1/32 and 100.65.0.102/32 (proto bgp, src 100.65.0.101).
  • The loopback-to-loopback ping works.

0.2 BMS1 has no tenant config yet [ optional ]

List the interfaces, VRFs and EVPN VNIs on BMS1:

docker exec -it bms1 ip -br link
docker exec -it bms1 ip vrf show
docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show evpn vni"

vtap0 and vtap1 (the links to vm1-red and vm1-green) exist, but they are not attached to anything. There is no VRF yet. FRR shows only VNI 1000 (type L3) from its own config, with no VXLAN interface and tenant VRF Unknown.

0.3 EVPN routes from the other leaves [ optional ]

Show the EVPN type-3 (multicast) and type-5 (prefix) routes that BMS1 receives:

docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn route type multicast"
docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn route type prefix"

BGP already receives routes from BMS2 and BMS-DHCP: type-3 (one per VNI per VTEP) and type-5 (subnets of VRF LAB2). They are not used yet, because BMS1 has no matching VNI or VRF.

Task 1 – Create the VRF

Open a shell on BMS1:

docker exec -it bms1 bash

Create VRF LAB2 with routing table 101 and bring it up:

ip link add LAB2 type vrf table 101
ip link set LAB2 up addrgen none

addrgen none disables automatic IPv6 link-local address generation. The VRF device, bridge ports and VXLAN devices do not need their own addresses.

Verify:

ip vrf show                      # LAB2 -> table 101
ip -d link show LAB2

ip -d link show LAB2 shows vrf table 101.

Task 2 – Create one bridge per network and put them in the VRF

On BMS1 each network gets its own, non-VLAN-aware bridge:

  • br-red: L2 segment red (VNI 100), with gateway 192.168.1.1
  • br-green: L2 segment green (VNI 200), with gateway 192.168.2.1
  • br-l3: the L3 VNI bridge (VNI 1000). It has no IP address.
ip link add br-red type bridge
ip link add br-green type bridge
ip link add br-l3 type bridge

Put the bridges in the VRF. The bridge interface itself works as the SVI, so its IP address and connected route belong to table 101:

ip link set br-l3 master LAB2
ip link set br-red master LAB2
ip link set br-green master LAB2

Verify:

ip -d link show br-red           # "bridge ... vlan_filtering 0"
ip link show master LAB2         # br-red, br-green, br-l3

Task 3 – Connect the VMs to the bridges

vtap0 goes to vm1-red and vtap1 goes to vm1-green:

ip link set vtap0 master br-red addrgen none
ip link set vtap1 master br-green addrgen none

Verify:

bridge link show                 # vtap0 master br-red, vtap1 master br-green
ip link show master br-red
ip link show master br-green

Task 4 – Configure the gateways (SVIs)

Assign the anycast gateway addresses to the red and green bridges:

ip addr add 192.168.1.1/24 dev br-red
ip addr add 192.168.2.1/24 dev br-green

Set the MAC addresses and bring the bridges up:

ip link set br-red addr 00:00:5e:00:10:01 up
ip link set br-green addr 00:00:5e:00:10:01 up
ip link set br-l3 addr 00:00:5e:00:f1:01 up
  • br-red / br-green: all leaves use the same gateway IP and the same gateway MAC (00:00:5e:00:10:01). This is called a distributed anycast gateway. A VM always sees the same default gateway, whichever leaf it is connected to.
  • br-l3: its MAC is this leaf's router MAC (RMAC). BGP sends it in EVPN type-2 and type-5 routes. Remote leaves use it as the inner destination MAC when they route traffic to this leaf. The RMAC must be unique per leaf: BMS1 …f1:01, BMS2 …f1:02, BMS-DHCP …f0:01. If two leaves had the same RMAC, each would reject the other's routes.

Verify:

ip -br addr show vrf LAB2        # br-red and br-green has IP assigned
ip -br link show master LAB2     # MAC matches, br-l3 being down is expected
ip route show vrf LAB2           # connected 192.168.1.0/24 and 192.168.2.0/24

Task 5 – Create the VXLAN interfaces and attach them to the bridges

Create one VXLAN device per VNI. dstport 4789 is the standard VXLAN UDP port. nolearning disables data-plane MAC learning on the VXLAN device: EVPN (FRR) installs the remote MACs instead.

ip link add vx-l3 type vxlan dstport 4789 vni 1000 nolearning
ip link add vx-red type vxlan dstport 4789 vni 100 nolearning
ip link add vx-green type vxlan dstport 4789 vni 200 nolearning

Attach each one to its bridge and bring it up:

ip link set vx-l3 master br-l3 addrgenmode none
ip link set vx-red master br-red addrgenmode none
ip link set vx-green master br-green addrgenmode none
ip link set vx-l3 up
ip link set vx-red up
ip link set vx-green up

Disable MAC learning on the VXLAN bridge ports. FRR installs the remote MACs on these ports:

bridge link set dev vx-red learning off
bridge link set dev vx-green learning off
bridge link set dev vx-l3 learning off

Verify:

ip -d link show vx-red           # "vxlan id 100 ... dstport 4789 nolearning"
ip -d link show vx-l3            # "vxlan id 1000 ..."
bridge link show                 # vx-red -> br-red, vx-green -> br-green, vx-l3 -> br-l3
ip link show master br-red       # vtap0 + vx-red

The data plane on BMS1 now looks like this:

VRF LAB2 (table 101)
 ├── br-red   192.168.1.1/24  [vtap0, vx-red   (VNI 100)]
 ├── br-green 192.168.2.1/24  [vtap1, vx-green (VNI 200)]
 └── br-l3    (no IP, RMAC)   [vx-l3 (VNI 1000)]

Task 6 – Let FRR pick up the new configuration

The FRR config has vrf LAB2 / vni 1000. The VRF and vx-l3 did not exist when FRR started, so reload FRR to apply the config again:

sv reload /services/frr

Wait about 15 seconds for EVPN to converge.

6.1 VNIs in FRR

Check the VNIs that FRR now knows on BMS1:

vtysh -c "show evpn vni"
vtysh -c "show vrf vni"
vtysh -c "show evpn vni 100"
vtysh -c "show evpn vni 1000"

Expected result:

  • VNI 100 and 200 are type L2 (VXLAN IF vx-red / vx-green), and VNI 1000 is type L3 (vx-l3). The tenant VRF of all three is LAB2.
  • VNI 100 and 200 each have two remote VTEPs: 100.65.0.1 and 100.65.0.102.
  • show evpn vni 1000 shows Router MAC 00:00:5e:00:f1:01 (the MAC of br-l3).

6.2 EVPN routes in BGP [ optional ]

Check EVPN routes from FRR perspective:

vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn summary"                # BGP session should be established
vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn route type multicast"   # type-3: VTEP membership per VNI
vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn route type macip"       # MAC / MAC+IP of hosts
vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn route type prefix"      # type-5: subnets in VRF LAB2
vtysh -c "show bgp vrf LAB2 ipv4 unicast"

You should now also see type-3 routes originated by 100.65.0.101 (BMS1).

6.3 Remote VTEPs and router MACs [ optional ]

Check VTEP and MACs from FRR perspective:

vtysh -c "show evpn rmac vni all"
vtysh -c "show evpn next-hops vni all"

Expected result: one RMAC, 00:00:5e:00:f0:01 → 100.65.0.1 (BMS-DHCP). BMS-DHCP is the only leaf with a subnet BMS1 doesn't have (orange, 192.168.3.0/24). BMS2 has the same subnets as BMS1, so its type-5 routes are never best on BMS1. BMS2's RMAC (00:00:5e:00:f1:02) shows up in Task 7, after BMS1 learns a host behind BMS2 through a type-2 MAC+IP route.

6.4 What FRR programmed into the kernel

The flood list (BUM traffic, head-end replication) is built from type-3 routes. It is stored as all-zero MAC entries on each L2 VXLAN device:

bridge fdb show dev vx-red | grep 00:00:00:00:00:00
# 00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 100.65.0.1 self permanent
# 00:00:00:00:00:00 dst 100.65.0.102 self permanent

Routing to other leaves goes through the L3 VNI. Remote prefixes point to the remote VTEP address onlink via br-l3. A static neighbor entry and an FDB entry map that address to the remote RMAC:

ip route show vrf LAB2                     # e.g. 192.168.3.0/24 via 100.65.0.1 dev br-l3 proto bgp ... onlink
ip neigh show dev br-l3                    # 100.65.0.1 lladdr 00:00:5e:00:f0:01 extern_learn
bridge fdb show dev vx-l3                  # 00:00:5e:00:f0:01 dst 100.65.0.1 ... extern_learn

extern_learn means that the entry was installed by the control plane (FRR/zebra), not learned from the data plane.

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

Task 7 – Test from the VMs

Keep a capture of the VXLAN traffic running on BMS1 during this task:

# Separate terminal
docker exec -it bms1 tcpdump -nei eth1 udp port 4789

7.1 DHCP over the L2 VNI

vm1-red and vm1-green have no IP address. Their DHCP servers are connected to BMS-DHCP. The DHCP broadcast reaches them only because BMS1 floods it over VNI 100 / 200 to all remote VTEPs (the flood list from Task 6.4).

Optionally, watch the DHCP server side:

# Separate terminal
docker exec -it dhcp-red tcpdump -nei eth1 port 67 or port 68

Request the leases:

docker exec -it vm1-red udhcpc -q -i eth1
docker exec -it vm1-green udhcpc -q -i eth1

Verify:

docker exec -it vm1-red ip addr show eth1        # 192.168.1.x/24 from the 10–100 pool
docker exec -it vm1-red ip route                 # default via 192.168.1.1
docker exec -it vm1-green ip addr show eth1      # 192.168.2.x/24
docker exec -it vm1-green ip route               # default via 192.168.2.1

In the BMS1 capture you should see VXLAN ... vni 100 (and vni 200) frames that carry the DHCP broadcast to 100.65.0.1 and 100.65.0.102.

7.2 Gateway and bridging (same subnet, other leaf)

Ping the local gateway, and the VM in the same subnet behind BMS2:

docker exec -it vm1-red ping -c 3 192.168.1.1        # local anycast gateway on BMS1
docker exec -it vm1-red ping -c 3 192.168.1.202      # vm2-red behind BMS2 – bridged over VNI 100
docker exec -it vm1-green ping -c 3 192.168.2.202    # vm2-green behind BMS2 – bridged over VNI 200

All three pings must work (0% packet loss). In the BMS1 capture the pings to BMS2 show up as vni 100 and vni 200.

7.3 Routing between subnets

Ping from red to green, and fetch the web page from the orange network:

docker exec -it vm1-red ping -c 3 192.168.2.202      # red -> green
docker exec -it vm1-red curl http://192.168.3.200    # red -> orange (www)
docker exec -it vm1-green curl http://192.168.3.200  # green -> orange (www)

curl must return the page This is a NGINX at: www-orange.

The orange network (VNI 300) exists only on BMS-DHCP. BMS1 has no br-orange, so it routes this traffic in VRF LAB2 and sends it over the L3 VNI. In the capture you should see vni 1000, with the inner destination MAC set to the RMAC of BMS-DHCP (00:00:5e:00:f0:01).

7.4 MAC/IP learning after the traffic [ optional ]

Check the topology MAC and IP from Linux and EVPN perspective:

docker exec -it bms1 bridge fdb show br br-red | grep -v permanent
docker exec -it bms1 ip neigh show vrf LAB2
docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show evpn mac vni 100"
docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show evpn arp-cache vni 100"
docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn route type macip"
docker exec -it vm2-red ping -c 1 192.168.1.1         # make BMS2 learn vm2-red's IP
docker exec -it bms1 vtysh -c "show evpn rmac vni all"  # now also 00:00:5e:00:f1:02 -> 100.65.0.102
docker exec -it bms1 ip route show vrf LAB2             # 192.168.1.202 via 100.65.0.102 dev br-l3 ... onlink
  • The MAC of vm1-red is learned locally on vtap0. FRR advertises it as a type-2 route.
  • The MACs of vm2-red and dhcp-red are on vx-red as extern_learn entries with dst 100.65.0.102 / dst 100.65.0.1. FRR installed them from type-2 routes.

Task 8 – Compare with the VLAN-aware bridge on BMS2 [ optional ]

BMS2 and BMS-DHCP build the same service with one VLAN-aware bridge br0 (vlan_filtering 1):

  • Each network is a VLAN on br0.
  • The SVIs (br-red, br-green, br-l3) are VLAN sub-interfaces of br0.
  • Each VXLAN device is a bridge port with its VLAN set as pvid untagged. This is how VLAN 100 maps to VNI 100, VLAN 200 to VNI 200, and VLAN 1000 to VNI 1000.

Look at the bridge, the VLANs and the FDB on BMS2:

docker exec -it bms2 ip -d link show br0            # "vlan_filtering 1"
docker exec -it bms2 ip -d link show br-red         # "vlan protocol 802.1Q id 100" on top of br0
docker exec -it bms2 bridge vlan show               # VLANs per port (PVID / Egress Untagged)
docker exec -it bms2 bridge vlan show dev vx-red    # vx-red: VLAN 100 PVID untagged
docker exec -it bms2 bridge fdb show br br0 vlan 100
docker exec -it bms2 bridge fdb show dev vx-red     # remote MACs + flood list (00:00:00:00:00:00)
Item BMS1 (this lab) BMS2 / BMS-DHCP
Bridges one per network (br-red, br-green, br-l3) one VLAN-aware br0
SVI the bridge itself VLAN sub-interface of br0 (br-red = br0.100)
VNI mapping VXLAN device is a port of the bridge VXLAN device port with pvid untagged VLAN
VM port mapping port of the bridge port with pvid untagged VLAN
FDB lookup key MAC (per bridge) MAC + VLAN

Both models work the same for FRR: zebra finds the VNI → bridge/VLAN → SVI mapping in the kernel.

Troubleshooting checklist

Symptom Check (on BMS1)
show evpn vni is empty or shows no L3 VNI ip link show master LAB2, bridge link show, then sv reload /services/frr again
No remote VTEPs on VNI 100/200 vtysh -c "show bgp l2vpn evpn summary", bridge fdb show dev vx-red
DHCP does not work ip link show master br-red (vtap0 + vx-red), flood list on vx-red
Same-subnet ping works, routing does not ip route show vrf LAB2, ip neigh show dev br-l3, vtysh -c "show evpn rmac vni all"
Remote type-5 routes are not installed MAC of br-l3 must be unique per leaf
No VXLAN packets on eth1 ip route (loopbacks via 10.1.0.x, src 100.65.0.101)

Cleanup

Destroy the lab:

containerlab destroy -t lab2.clab.yml

LAB 3 – Alternative DP - OVS/OVN

Goals

In this lab you build the same tenant network as in LAB 2 (red, green and orange networks connected by a router). This time you use OVN on top of Open vSwitch instead of BGP EVPN. You configure the whole network from one place (BMS1). After this lab you should be able to:

  • explain the roles of OVS (br-int, OpenFlow, Geneve tunnels) and OVN (Northbound DB, ovn-northd, Southbound DB, ovn-controller),
  • create logical switches (L2 networks) and connect VM ports to them,
  • create a logical router and connect it to the switches,
  • use OVN's native DHCP, with no separate DHCP server,
  • check the result in the OVN databases, in OVS and on the wire, and trace a packet with ovn-trace.

Topology

Logical topology

The logical topology you build:

Tenant networks

Network Logical switch Subnet Router port / gateway DHCP
red red 192.168.1.0/24 lrp-red 192.168.1.1, 02:ac:10:0a:00:01 OVN native, for vm1-red
green green 192.168.2.0/24 lrp-green 192.168.2.1, 02:ac:10:0a:14:01 OVN native, for vm1-green
orange orange 192.168.3.0/24 lrp-orange 192.168.3.1, 02:ac:10:0a:1e:01 options created, not used

Hosts

Node Address MAC (eth1) Connected to OVN logical port (iface-id)
vm1-red DHCP → .1.201 02:0a:0a:00:10:11 BMS1 vtap0 vm1-red
vm1-green DHCP → .2.201 02:0a:0a:00:20:11 BMS1 vtap1 vm1-green
vm2-red 192.168.1.202/24 random BMS2 vtap0 vm2-red
vm2-green 192.168.2.202/24 random BMS2 vtap1 vm2-green
vm3-red 192.168.1.203/24 random BMS3 vtap0 vm3-red
vm3-green 192.168.2.203/24 random BMS3 vtap1 vm3-green
www 192.168.3.200/24 random BMS3 vtap2 www

Management addresses (network 172.16.0.0/24): BMS1 .11, BMS2 .12, BMS3 .13, vm1-red .21, vm1-green .22, vm2-red .23, vm2-green .24, vm3-red .31, vm3-green .32, www .33, l2-switch .40.

OVN components

Component Where Role
Northbound DB BMS1 (TCP 6641) The desired logical network: switches, routers, ports, DHCP. You write here with ovn-nbctl.
ovn-northd BMS1 Translates the NB DB into logical flows in the SB DB.
Southbound DB BMS1 (TCP 6642) Logical flows, chassis list, port bindings, MAC bindings.
ovn-controller every BMS Connects to the SB DB on BMS1. Programs OpenFlow on its local br-int and creates the Geneve tunnels.
OVS (br-int) every BMS The data plane. VM ports (vtapX) and tunnel ports are attached here.

For simplicity all BMS nodes use the same image, so BMS2 and BMS3 also run their own NB/SB DB and ovn-northd. These are not used: every ovn-controller connects to tcp:10.1.0.101:6642 (BMS1). Run all ovn-nbctl and ovn-sbctl commands on BMS1.

What is already configured when the lab starts:

  • OVS and OVN services on BMS1, BMS2 and BMS3. Each chassis has a system-id (BMS1, BMS2, BMS3), ovn-encap-type=geneve and its own ovn-encap-ip.
  • The VM ports vtapX are added to br-int. Each one has external-ids:iface-id=<logical port name>. When a logical port with that name appears in OVN, the chassis that has the interface claims it.
  • Static addresses on vm2-, vm3- and www. vm1-red and vm1-green have fixed MAC addresses but no IP address.

Your job is to create the logical network in the OVN Northbound DB on BMS1.

Deploying the lab and accessing nodes

Go to the lab directory, deploy the lab and list its nodes:

cd lab3
containerlab deploy -t lab3.clab.yml
containerlab inspect -t lab3.clab.yml

containerlab inspect lists eleven nodes in state running, with their management IP addresses.

To open a shell on a node:

docker exec -it bms1 bash        # BMS nodes have bash
docker exec -it vm1-red sh
# or
ssh root@172.16.0.11             # BMS1 via its management IP

Note: Do not run ./setup.sh or /tmp/setup.sh. Those scripts are the reference solution. In this lab you type every command yourself.

Task 0 – Check the starting point

0.1 OVS on each BMS [ optional ]

Show the OVS bridge, the VM port settings and the OVN settings of BMS1:

docker exec -it bms1 ovs-vsctl show
docker exec -it bms1 ovs-vsctl --columns=name,external_ids list Interface vtap0 vtap1
docker exec -it bms1 ovs-vsctl get Open_vSwitch . external_ids

Expected result:

  • br-int has the ports vtap0 and vtap1.
  • There are tunnel ports of type geneve to the other chassis (remote_ip="10.1.0.102", remote_ip="10.1.0.103").
  • vtap0 has iface-id=vm1-red, and vtap1 has iface-id=vm1-green.
  • external_ids has system-id=BMS1, ovn-remote="tcp:10.1.0.101:6642", ovn-encap-type=geneve and ovn-encap-ip="10.1.0.101".

You might want run the same commands on bms2 and bms3. BMS3 also has vtap2 (iface-id=www).

0.2 Chassis registered in the Southbound DB

Show the chassis that are registered in the Southbound DB:

docker exec -it bms1 ovn-sbctl show

Expected result: three chassis, BMS1, BMS2 and BMS3, each with a geneve encap on its 10.1.0.10x address. No port is bound yet.

0.3 The Northbound DB is empty [ optional ]

Show the logical network in the Northbound DB:

docker exec -it bms1 ovn-nbctl show

The output is empty. No logical switches or routers exist yet.

0.4 Underlay [ optional ]

Ping the tunnel (encap) addresses of BMS2 and BMS3 from BMS1:

docker exec -it bms1 ping -c 3 10.1.0.102
docker exec -it bms1 ping -c 3 10.1.0.103

Both pings must work (0% packet loss). The Geneve tunnels use these addresses.

Task 1 – Create the logical switches

Open a shell on BMS1 for Tasks 1–6:

docker exec -it bms1 bash

Each logical switch is one L2 network, the same as a bridge/VLAN plus L2 VNI in LAB 2. It spans all chassis automatically.

ovn-nbctl ls-add red
ovn-nbctl ls-add green
ovn-nbctl ls-add orange

Verify [ optional ]:

ovn-nbctl ls-list
ovn-nbctl show

Both commands list the three switches green, orange and red. They have no ports yet.

Task 2 – Create the logical router

Create the logical router lr-bms. It routes between the three networks:

ovn-nbctl lr-add lr-bms

Verify [ optional ]:

ovn-nbctl lr-list

The output lists one router, lr-bms.

Task 3 – Add router ports (one per network)

Each logical router port has a MAC address and the gateway IP of its network:

ovn-nbctl lrp-add lr-bms lrp-red    02:ac:10:0a:00:01 192.168.1.1/24
ovn-nbctl lrp-add lr-bms lrp-green  02:ac:10:0a:14:01 192.168.2.1/24
ovn-nbctl lrp-add lr-bms lrp-orange 02:ac:10:0a:1e:01 192.168.3.1/24

Verify [ optional ]:

ovn-nbctl show lr-bms
ovn-nbctl lrp-list lr-bms
ovn-nbctl lr-route-list lr-bms

lr-route-list is empty. The three subnets are directly connected to the router, so they need no static routes.

Task 4 – Connect the switches to the router

Each switch needs a port of type router that is the peer of a router port:

  • lsp-set-type ... router: this switch port connects to a logical router.
  • lsp-set-options ... router-port=lrp-xxx: the router port on the other side.
  • lsp-set-addresses ... router: take the MAC/IP from the peer router port. With this, the switch can answer ARP for the gateway and send gateway-bound frames to the router.
ovn-nbctl lsp-add red lsp-rt-red
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-type lsp-rt-red router
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-options lsp-rt-red router-port=lrp-red
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses lsp-rt-red router

ovn-nbctl lsp-add green lsp-rt-green
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-type lsp-rt-green router
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-options lsp-rt-green router-port=lrp-green
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses lsp-rt-green router

ovn-nbctl lsp-add orange lsp-rt-orange
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-type lsp-rt-orange router
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-options lsp-rt-orange router-port=lrp-orange
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses lsp-rt-orange router

Verify [ optional ]:

ovn-nbctl show
ovn-nbctl lsp-list red
ovn-nbctl lsp-get-type lsp-rt-red          # router
ovn-nbctl lsp-get-options lsp-rt-red       # router-port=lrp-red

In ovn-nbctl show, each switch now has a port lsp-rt-xxx with type: router and router-port: lrp-xxx.

Task 5 – Create the DHCP options

OVN has a built-in DHCP server. ovn-controller answers DHCP requests locally, on the chassis where the VM is connected, so no DHCP server container is needed. A DHCP_Options row describes one subnet. The options server_id, server_mac and lease_time are mandatory.

ovn-nbctl create prints the UUID of the new row. Save it in a shell variable, because you need it here and in Task 6:

DHCP_RED=$(ovn-nbctl create DHCP_Options cidr=192.168.1.0/24)
DHCP_GREEN=$(ovn-nbctl create DHCP_Options cidr=192.168.2.0/24)
DHCP_ORANGE=$(ovn-nbctl create DHCP_Options cidr=192.168.3.0/24)

Configure all required options:

ovn-nbctl dhcp-options-set-options $DHCP_RED  lease_time=3600 router=192.168.1.1 server_id=192.168.1.1 server_mac=c0:ff:ee:00:00:01
ovn-nbctl dhcp-options-set-options $DHCP_GREEN  lease_time=3600 router=192.168.2.1 server_id=192.168.2.1 server_mac=c0:ff:ee:00:00:01

Verify:

echo $DHCP_RED $DHCP_GREEN
ovn-nbctl dhcp-options-list
ovn-nbctl dhcp-options-get-options $DHCP_RED

dhcp-options-list shows three UUIDs, the same as in the echo output. dhcp-options-get-options shows lease_time=3600, router=192.168.1.1, server_id=192.168.1.1 and server_mac=c0:ff:ee:00:00:01.

If you lose the shell variables (for example after opening a new shell), find the UUID again: DHCP_RED=$(ovn-nbctl --bare --columns=_uuid find DHCP_Options cidr="192.168.1.0/24")

Task 6 – Add the VM ports

The name of each logical switch port must match the iface-id that is set on the vtapX interface of the chassis. This is how OVN knows where each port is.

The VMs use two kinds of addresses:

  • vm1-red / vm1-green: the MAC and IP are known ("<mac> <ip>"). OVN uses them for the DHCP reply. ovn-controller answers ARP for them and delivers frames to them by MAC.
  • vm2-*, vm3-*, www: unknown. OVN does not know their addresses. Frames to unknown MAC addresses are delivered to these ports. The router learns their MAC from ARP and stores it in the MAC_Binding table.

6.1 red

Add the three VM ports of the red network. Only vm1-red gets DHCP:

ovn-nbctl lsp-add red vm1-red
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses vm1-red "02:0a:0a:00:10:11 192.168.1.201"
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-dhcpv4-options vm1-red "$DHCP_RED"

ovn-nbctl lsp-add red vm2-red
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses vm2-red unknown

ovn-nbctl lsp-add red vm3-red
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses vm3-red unknown

6.2 green

Add the three VM ports of the green network. Only vm1-green gets DHCP:

ovn-nbctl lsp-add green vm1-green
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses vm1-green "02:0a:0a:00:20:11 192.168.2.201"
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-dhcpv4-options vm1-green "$DHCP_GREEN"

ovn-nbctl lsp-add green vm2-green
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses vm2-green unknown

ovn-nbctl lsp-add green vm3-green
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses vm3-green unknown

6.3 orange

Add the port of the web server:

ovn-nbctl lsp-add orange www
ovn-nbctl lsp-set-addresses www unknown

6.4 Wait until all chassis have applied the config

ovn-nbctl --wait=hv sync

--wait=hv returns when every ovn-controller has installed the new configuration into its OVS.

Verify the Northbound DB:

ovn-nbctl show
ovn-nbctl lsp-get-addresses vm1-red
ovn-nbctl lsp-get-dhcpv4-options vm1-red

lsp-get-addresses shows 02:0a:0a:00:10:11 192.168.1.201, and lsp-get-dhcpv4-options shows the UUID of DHCP_RED with (192.168.1.0/24).

Task 7 – Check the Southbound DB and OVS

7.1 Port bindings

Show the chassis and the ports bound to them:

ovn-sbctl show

Expected result: each chassis has claimed the ports of its VMs:

Chassis Ports
BMS1 vm1-red, vm1-green
BMS2 vm2-red, vm2-green
BMS3 vm3-red, vm3-green, www

7.2 Datapaths and logical flows [ optional ]

ovn-northd creates one datapath per logical switch and router. Each one has a tunnel key, which is also used as the Geneve VNI:

ovn-sbctl --columns=external_ids,tunnel_key list Datapath_Binding
ovn-sbctl lflow-list red | head -40
ovn-sbctl lflow-list lr-bms | grep -c table

There are four datapaths: red, green, orange and lr-bms, each with its own tunnel_key. The router alone has more than a hundred logical flows.

7.3 OpenFlow programmed by ovn-controller [ optional ]

ovn-controller turns the logical flows into OpenFlow rules on br-int:

ovs-ofctl dump-flows br-int | wc -l
ovs-vsctl show                                   # br-int, vtap0, vtap1 and the geneve ports
ovs-vsctl --columns=name,ofport list Interface   # OpenFlow port numbers

br-int now has several hundred OpenFlow rules, even for this small network.

7.4 ovn-trace

ovn-trace simulates a packet through the logical pipeline and shows each logical table it passes. Trace a packet from vm1-red to www:

ovn-trace --summary red 'inport == "vm1-red" && eth.src == 02:0a:0a:00:10:11 && eth.dst == 02:ac:10:0a:00:01 && ip4.src == 192.168.1.201 && ip4.dst == 192.168.3.200 && ip.ttl == 64'

Expected result: the packet enters switch red, goes to lr-bms through lsp-rt-red → lrp-red, is routed (TTL decremented) out of lrp-orange into switch orange, and is output to port www. If OVN does not know the MAC of 192.168.3.200 yet, the trace ends with an ARP request from the router.

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

Task 8 – Test from the VMs

In separate terminal keep a capture of the Geneve traffic running on BMS1 during this task:

# Separate terminal
docker exec -it bms1 tcpdump -nei eth1 udp port 6081

8.1 OVN native DHCP

Request a DHCP lease on vm1-red and vm1-green:

docker exec -it vm1-red udhcpc -q -i eth1
docker exec -it vm1-green udhcpc -q -i eth1

Verify:

docker exec -it vm1-red ip addr show eth1        # 192.168.1.201/24
docker exec -it vm1-red ip route                 # default via 192.168.1.1
docker exec -it vm1-green ip addr show eth1      # 192.168.2.201/24
docker exec -it vm1-green ip route               # default via 192.168.2.1

The DHCP reply comes from server_mac c0:ff:ee:00:00:01 and is generated by ovn-controller on BMS1. The Geneve capture shows no DHCP packets, because nothing leaves BMS1.

8.2 Gateway and L2 (same subnet, other chassis)

Ping the router port, and the VMs in the same subnet on BMS2 and BMS3. All pings must work (0% packet loss):

docker exec -it vm1-red ping -c 3 192.168.1.1        # logical router port
docker exec -it vm1-red ping -c 3 192.168.1.202      # vm2-red on BMS2
docker exec -it vm1-red ping -c 3 192.168.1.203      # vm3-red on BMS3
docker exec -it vm1-green ping -c 3 192.168.2.202    # vm2-green on BMS2
docker exec -it vm1-green ping -c 3 192.168.2.203    # vm3-green on BMS3

In the capture, the traffic to vm2-red / vm3-red goes in Geneve packets to 10.1.0.102 / 10.1.0.103.

8.3 Routing between subnets

Ping from red to green, and fetch the web page from the orange network:

docker exec -it vm1-red ping -c 3 192.168.2.202      # red -> green
docker exec -it vm1-red curl http://192.168.3.200    # red -> orange (www)
docker exec -it vm1-green curl http://192.168.3.200  # green -> orange (www)

curl must return the page This is a NGINX at: www-orange.

The logical router is distributed. The packet is routed on BMS1, the chassis where it enters, and goes in a Geneve packet directly to BMS3. In the capture, the inner frame already has the router MAC 02:ac:10:0a:1e:01 as source and a decremented TTL.

8.4 What OVN learned [ optional ]

Check MACs that OVN learned due to previous steps:

docker exec -it bms1 ovn-sbctl --columns=logical_port,ip,mac list MAC_Binding

MAC_Binding holds the MACs that the router learned through ARP when it routed traffic: 192.168.3.200 (www) on lrp-orange, 192.168.2.202 (vm2-green) on lrp-green, and the return path to vm1-red and vm1-green. Same-subnet traffic (Task 8.2) does not go through the router, so vm2-red and vm3-* are not listed.

OVN vs. EVPN (LAB 2 vs LAB 3)

This table compares two approches:

Item LAB 2 – EVPN/VXLAN (FRR + Linux) LAB 3 – OVN/OVS
Control plane Distributed: BGP EVPN between leaves, with an RR Central: NB/SB OVSDB on BMS1, ovn-northd
Where you configure Every leaf (VRF, bridges, VXLAN, FRR) Only BMS1 (ovn-nbctl)
Encapsulation VXLAN (UDP 4789), VNI per network Geneve (UDP 6081), tunnel key per datapath
L2 network Linux bridge (or VLAN) + L2 VNI Logical switch
Gateway / routing Anycast SVI on every leaf + L3 VNI (symmetric IRB) Distributed logical router (routed on the ingress chassis)
MAC/IP distribution Learned locally, advertised as type-2/type-5 routes Set in NB (lsp-set-addresses), or learned by ARP (MAC_Binding)
BUM traffic Head-end replication, flood list from type-3 routes Replication to the chassis that have ports on the switch
DHCP Separate DHCP server containers, reached over L2 VNI Native, answered locally by ovn-controller
Data plane Linux kernel (bridge, vxlan, VRF) OVS kernel datapath, programmed with OpenFlow

Troubleshooting checklist

Symptom Check (on BMS1)
A chassis is missing in ovn-sbctl show On that BMS: ovs-vsctl get Open_vSwitch . external_ids, sv status /services/ovn-controller
A port is not bound (chassis empty) The LSP name must match iface-id on the BMS: ovs-vsctl --columns=name,external_ids list Interface
No DHCP lease ovn-nbctl lsp-get-dhcpv4-options vm1-red, ovn-nbctl lsp-get-addresses vm1-red (the MAC must match the VM's eth1)
Same-subnet ping to BMS2/BMS3 fails ovs-vsctl show (geneve ports), ping 10.1.0.102
Routing fails ovn-nbctl show lr-bms, the lsp-rt-* options, then ovn-trace
ovn-nbctl hangs sv status /services/ovsdb-server-ovn /services/ovn-northd

Logs: /var/log/ovn/ovn-controller.log, /var/log/ovn/ovn-northd.log, /var/log/openvswitch/ovs-vswitchd.log.

Cleanup

Destroy the lab:

containerlab destroy -t lab3.clab.yml

LAB 4 – DPDK & VPP

Goals

In this lab you connect three routers. Each router has VPP as the data plane and FRR in Linux as the control plane. You build the links between them by hand. After this lab you should be able to:

  • create a memif link between two VPP instances (shared memory, master / slave),
  • create a vhost-user interface in VPP (backend) and connect a DPDK virtio_user device (frontend) to it,
  • run DPDK testpmd as a transparent "cable" between two virtio_user ports,
  • use the VPP linux-cp plugin to mirror VPP interfaces into Linux as TAP interfaces, and see how IP addresses, routes and ARP entries are synced from the kernel (FRR) into the VPP FIB,
  • check the result in VPP (vppctl), in Linux (ip) and in FRR (vtysh).

Topology

Addressing

Node VPP interface Linux TAP (linux-cp) Address Peer
R1 loop0 lo-lcp 100.65.0.1/32 –
memif1/1 (slave) tap1 10.1.0.1/30 R2 memif1/1
R2 loop0 lo-lcp 100.65.0.2/32 –
memif1/1 (master) tap1 10.1.0.2/30 R1 memif1/1
VirtualEthernet0/0/0 tap0 10.2.0.2/30 L2 net_virtio_user0
R3 loop0 lo-lcp 100.65.0.3/32 –
VirtualEthernet0/0/0 tap0 10.2.0.1/30 L2 net_virtio_user1

Management addresses (network 172.16.0.0/24): R1 .11, R2 .12, R3 .13, L2 .40.

Control plane (FRR)

  • R1 ↔ R2: OSPF area 0 on tap1 (point-to-point). The loopbacks (lo-lcp) are passive.
  • R2 ↔ R3: eBGP, AS 65002 ↔ AS 65003, over tap0. Both routers advertise their loopback.
  • R2 redistributes BGP into OSPF and OSPF into BGP. R1 learns 100.65.0.3/32, and R3 learns 100.65.0.1/32.

How the pieces fit together

  • VPP owns the data-plane interfaces (memif1/1, VirtualEthernet0/0/0, loop0) and forwards packets in user space.

  • linux-cp creates a TAP pair for each VPP interface:

    • one end is in VPP (tap4096, tap4097, …),
    • the other end is in Linux (lo-lcp, tap1, tap0).

    Control-plane packets (OSPF, BGP, ARP, ping to the router itself) are punted from VPP to Linux through this pair. Packets that Linux sends go back out through VPP.

  • lcp-sync (in startup.conf): IP addresses, link state, routes and ARP neighbors that FRR/Linux set on the TAP interfaces are copied into VPP via netlink. FRR never talks to VPP directly; it only programs the Linux kernel.

  • memif: a shared-memory packet interface between two processes. The master creates the socket and the shared memory. The slave connects to it.

  • vhost-user / virtio_user: VPP is the vhost-user backend in server mode, so it creates the socket. testpmd uses DPDK virtio_user devices as the frontend (client). They connect to the sockets and share their memory with VPP.

  • testpmd in io forwarding mode sends everything from port 0 to port 1 and back, without changes. It works like a cable between R2 and R3.

What is already configured when the lab starts:

  • VPP on R1, R2 and R3, with the linux_cp, linux_nl and vhost plugins enabled and DPDK disabled.
  • loop0 in VPP, mirrored to Linux as lo-lcp (from /etc/vpp/vpp-exec.conf).
  • FRR. It starts only after VPP has finished its startup config. Its config already has sections for tap1 / tap0, but these interfaces do not exist yet.
  • The shared volume /var/run/vhost in all four containers, used for the memif and vhost-user sockets.

Your job is to create the memif and vhost-user interfaces, mirror them into Linux with linux-cp, and start testpmd.

Deploying the lab and accessing nodes

Go to the lab directory, deploy the lab and list its nodes:

cd lab4
containerlab deploy -t lab4.clab.yml
containerlab inspect -t lab4.clab.yml

containerlab inspect lists four nodes (l2, r1, r2, r3) in state running, with their management IP addresses.

To open a shell on a node:

docker exec -it r1 sh            # r1, r2, r3, l2
# or
ssh root@172.16.0.11             # R1 via its management IP

The VPP CLI on a router is vppctl <command>, or vppctl alone for an interactive prompt (vpp#). The FRR CLI is vtysh.

Tip: testpmd (Task 4) runs in the foreground and keeps its own prompt. Use a separate terminal for it and leave it running.

Note: Do not run ./setup.sh or /tmp/setup.sh. Those scripts are the reference solution. In this lab you type every command yourself.

Task 0 – Check the starting point

Run on each router r1 [ optional: r2, r3 ]:

docker exec -it r1 vppctl show version
docker exec -it r1 vppctl show interface
docker exec -it r1 vppctl show interface addr
docker exec -it r1 vppctl show lcp
docker exec -it r1 ip -br addr

Expected result (R1):

loop0 (up):
  L3 100.65.0.1/32
tap4096 (up):

lcp lcp-sync on
...
itf-pair: [0] loop0 tap4096 lo-lcp 3 type tap

lo-lcp           UP             100.65.0.1/32 ...
  • VPP has only local0, loop0 and tap4096, the VPP end of the linux-cp pair for loop0.
  • In Linux, lo-lcp has the loopback address, set by FRR.
  • 100.65.0.1/32 shows up on loop0 in VPP because of lcp-sync.

Check the shared socket directory:

docker exec -it l2 ls -la /var/run/vhost/

Socket files from an earlier run can stay in /var/run/vhost (it is a docker volume). This is fine: the master/server side creates them again.

Task 1 – R2: memif master towards R1 and vhost-user towards L2

Open a shell on R2:

docker exec -it r2 bash

1.1 Create the memif socket and the memif interface (master)

Create the memif socket file, a memif interface in master mode on it, and bring the interface up:

vppctl create memif socket id 1 filename /var/run/vhost/r1-r2-memif.sock
vppctl create interface memif id 1 socket-id 1 master
vppctl set int state memif1/1 up

The interface name memif1/1 is memif<socket-id>/<id>.

Verify:

vppctl show memif

Expected result: socket 1 is a listener (R2 is master). The interface is admin-up but not connected yet, with num-s2m-rings 0, because R1 does not exist on the other side yet.

sockets
  id  listener    filename
  1   yes (1)     /var/run/vhost/r1-r2-memif.sock

interface memif1/1
  socket-id 1 id 1 mode ethernet
  flags admin-up

1.2 Mirror memif1/1 into Linux as tap1

Create the linux-cp pair for memif1/1. The Linux end is called tap1:

vppctl lcp create memif1/1 host-if tap1

Verify:

vppctl show lcp | grep itf-pair
ip -br addr show tap1
vppctl show int addr

Expected result:

itf-pair: [1] memif1/1 tap4097 tap1 4 type tap

tap1             DOWN           10.1.0.2/30 ...  <NO-CARRIER,...,UP>

memif1/1 (up):
  L3 10.1.0.2/30
  • FRR sees the new tap1 and sets 10.1.0.2/30 on it right away.
  • lcp-sync copies the address to memif1/1 in VPP.
  • tap1 has NO-CARRIER, because linux-cp mirrors the link state of memif1/1, which is not connected yet.

1.3 Create the vhost-user interface (server) and mirror it as tap0

Create the vhost-user interface in server mode, bring it up and mirror it into Linux as tap0:

vppctl create vhost-user socket /var/run/vhost/r2-l2.sock server
vppctl set int state VirtualEthernet0/0/0 up
vppctl lcp create VirtualEthernet0/0/0 host-if tap0

create vhost-user prints the name of the new interface, VirtualEthernet0/0/0.

Verify:

vppctl show vhost-user
vppctl show int addr
ip -br addr show tap0

Expected result: socket filename /var/run/vhost/r2-l2.sock type server. Memory regions (total 0) and features (0x0), because no frontend is connected yet. VirtualEthernet0/0/0 has 10.2.0.2/30.

1.4 Reload FRR

Reload FRR on R2:

sv reload /services/frr

This makes FRR apply the whole config again (OSPF on tap1, BGP over tap0) now that the interfaces exist.

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

Task 2 – R1: memif slave towards R2

Open a shell on R1:

docker exec -it r1 bash

Create memif interface and add it to linux-cp and reload FRR:

vppctl create memif socket id 1 filename /var/run/vhost/r1-r2-memif.sock
vppctl create interface memif id 1 socket-id 1 slave
vppctl set int state memif1/1 up
vppctl lcp create memif1/1 host-if tap1
sv reload /services/frr

2.1 Verify the memif connection

Show the memif sockets and interfaces on R1:

vppctl show memif

Expected result: socket 1 is not a listener (R1 is slave). The interface is connected, and the rings and shared-memory regions are set up:

interface memif1/1
  remote-name "VPP 26.06-release"
  remote-interface "memif1/1"
  socket-id 1 id 1 mode ethernet
  flags admin-up slave connected zero-copy
  num-s2m-rings 1 num-m2s-rings 1 buffer-size 2048 num-regions 2

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

On R2, tap1 now has carrier:

docker exec -it r2 ip -br link show tap1      # UP ... <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP>
docker exec -it r2 vppctl show memif memif1/1 # connected

2.2 Verify the link and OSPF

Open again a shell on R1:

docker exec -it r1 bash

Check the address in VPP, ping R2 over the memif link and check the OSPF neighbor:

vppctl show int addr                 # memif1/1: L3 10.1.0.1/30
ping -c 2 10.1.0.2
vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"     # 100.65.0.2  Full/-  tap1

The ping must work (0% packet loss). OSPF needs up to about 40 seconds to reach Full.

2.3 Verify the kernel → VPP sync (linux-cp)

Compare the Linux tables with the VPP tables:

ip route                             # 100.65.0.2 via 10.1.0.2 dev tap1 proto ospf
vppctl show ip fib 100.65.0.2/32
ip neigh show dev tap1               # 10.1.0.2 lladdr 02:fe:... REACHABLE
vppctl show ip neighbors             # 10.1.0.2  D  02:fe:...  memif1/1

Expected result in the VPP FIB: the route has source lcp-rt-dynamic, and its path points to memif1/1, the VPP interface, not tap1:

100.65.0.2/32 fib:0 index:19 locks:2
  lcp-rt-dynamic refs:1 src-flags:added,contributing,active,
      ...
        10.1.0.2 memif1/1
      [@0]: ipv4 via 10.1.0.2 memif1/1: mtu:9000 ...

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

Task 3 – R3: vhost-user towards L2

Open a shell on R3:

docker exec -it r3 bash

Create vhost-user interface (server) and mirror it as tap0 interface and reload FRR at the end:

vppctl create vhost-user socket /var/run/vhost/r3-l2.sock server
vppctl set int state VirtualEthernet0/0/0 up
vppctl lcp create VirtualEthernet0/0/0 host-if tap0
sv reload /services/frr

Verify:

vppctl show int addr                 # VirtualEthernet0/0/0: L3 10.2.0.1/30
vppctl show vhost-user               # type server, Memory regions (total 0)
ip -br addr show tap0                # DOWN, 10.2.0.1/30

tap0 stays DOWN and the BGP session to R2 cannot come up yet: nothing connects the two vhost-user sockets.

Task 4 – L2: testpmd as a cable between R2 and R3

Open a new terminal and a shell on L2:

docker exec -it l2 bash

Start testpmd:

dpdk-testpmd --lcores='(0-1)@0' \
        --no-pci \
        --in-memory \
        --single-file-segments \
        --vdev 'net_virtio_user0,path=/var/run/vhost/r2-l2.sock,queues=1' \
        --vdev 'net_virtio_user1,path=/var/run/vhost/r3-l2.sock,queues=1' \
        -- -i --forward-mode=io --auto-start --total-num-mbufs=8192 --nb-cores=1
Option Meaning
--lcores='(0-1)@0' EAL: lcores 0 and 1 (main + 1 forwarding) both run on CPU 0
--no-pci EAL: do not scan or probe PCI devices
--in-memory EAL: no hugepage files or runtime files on disk
--single-file-segments EAL: fewer, larger memory files (needed to share memory with vhost-user)
--vdev 'net_virtio_user0,path=...' virtual device: virtio_user frontend connected to R2's vhost-user socket → port 0
--vdev 'net_virtio_user1,path=...' the same, connected to R3's socket → port 1
-- end of EAL options, start of testpmd options
-i interactive mode (testpmd> prompt)
--forward-mode=io forward port 0 ↔ port 1 without touching the packets
--auto-start start forwarding right away
--total-num-mbufs=8192 size of the packet buffer pool
--nb-cores=1 one forwarding core

At the testpmd> prompt, check:

testpmd> show port info all
testpmd> show config fwd
testpmd> show port stats all

Expected result: two ports, net_virtio_user0 (port 0) and net_virtio_user1 (port 1), both with link up. Forwarding mode is io, with the stream port 0 ↔ port 1. show port stats all shows RX/TX counters going up once the routers exchange traffic. Run it again later to see the counters grow.

Leave testpmd running. If you quit, the R2 ↔ R3 link goes down.

4.1 Verify the vhost-user side in VPP

In your first terminal exit docker shell if any:

exit

Then execute:

docker exec -it r2 vppctl show vhost-user
docker exec -it r2 ip -br link show tap0

Then execute [ optional ]:

docker exec -it r2 vppctl show hardware-interfaces VirtualEthernet0/0/0
docker exec -it r3 vppctl show vhost-user
docker exec -it r3 ip -br link show tap0

Expected result: the frontend has connected and negotiated virtio features (features (0x150008000), protocol features (0x1)). There is Memory regions (total 1), which is testpmd's memory mapped into VPP. The link is up, and tap0 is now UP ... LOWER_UP.

Task 5 – Check end-to-end routing

5.1 BGP R2 ↔ R3 [ optional ]

Check BGP status:

docker exec -it r3 vtysh -c "show bgp summary"
docker exec -it r3 vtysh -c "show ip route bgp"

Expected result:

Neighbor        V         AS   MsgRcvd   MsgSent   TblVer  InQ OutQ  Up/Down State/PfxRcd   PfxSnt
10.2.0.2        4      65002         6         6        3    0    0 00:00:19            2        3

B>* 100.65.0.1/32 [20/20] via 10.2.0.2, tap0, weight 1, 00:00:18
B>* 100.65.0.2/32 [20/0] via 10.2.0.2, tap0, weight 1, 00:00:18

5.2 OSPF on R1 (BGP routes redistributed by R2) [ optional ]

Check OSPF status:

docker exec -it r1 vtysh -c "show ip route ospf"

Expected result:

O>* 10.2.0.0/30 [110/20] via 10.1.0.2, tap1, weight 1
O>* 100.65.0.2/32 [110/20] via 10.1.0.2, tap1, weight 1
O>* 100.65.0.3/32 [110/20] via 10.1.0.2, tap1, weight 1

5.3 The same routes in VPP

Check that the routes learned by FRR are also in the VPP FIB:

docker exec -it r1 vppctl show ip fib 100.65.0.3/32     # lcp-rt-dynamic, via 10.1.0.2 memif1/1

[ optional ]:

docker exec -it r3 vppctl show ip fib 100.65.0.1/32     # lcp-rt-dynamic, via 10.2.0.2 VirtualEthernet0/0/0
docker exec -it r2 vppctl show ip fib                   # the full FIB of the transit router

5.4 Ping loopback to loopback

Ping between the loopbacks of R1 and R3, in both directions:

docker exec -it r1 ping -c 3 -I 100.65.0.1 100.65.0.3
docker exec -it r3 ping -c 3 -I 100.65.0.3 100.65.0.1

Expected result: replies with ttl=63, so one hop (R2) routed the packet.

Task 6 – Follow a packet through the VPP graph on R2 [ optional ]

R2 forwards R1 ↔ R3 traffic entirely in VPP. The Linux kernel on R2 never sees these packets. Check this with a VPP packet trace:

docker exec -it r2 vppctl clear trace
docker exec -it r2 vppctl trace add memif-input 5
docker exec -it r1 ping -c 1 -I 100.65.0.1 100.65.0.3
docker exec -it r2 vppctl show trace

Expected path of the echo request through the VPP graph nodes:

memif-input
ethernet-input
ip4-input
ip4-lookup
ip4-rewrite
VirtualEthernet0/0/0-output
VirtualEthernet0/0/0-tx

The packet comes in on memif, is routed with the FIB entry that linux-cp synced from FRR, and leaves on the vhost-user interface. It does not pass through tap* or linux-cp-* nodes.

To trace the opposite direction (from R3), use the vhost-user input node:

docker exec -it r2 vppctl clear trace
docker exec -it r2 vppctl trace add vhost-user-input 5
docker exec -it r3 ping -c 1 -I 100.65.0.3 100.65.0.1
docker exec -it r2 vppctl show trace

Other useful VPP commands:

docker exec -it r2 vppctl show runtime            # per-node counters (memif-input, vhost-user-input, *-tx)
docker exec -it r2 vppctl show errors             # drop / error counters
docker exec -it r2 vppctl show interface          # rx/tx counters per interface

In the testpmd terminal, show port stats all now shows the forwarded packets on both ports.

Troubleshooting checklist

Symptom Check
memif1/1 not connected Both sides use the same socket file. R2 is master and R1 is slave. vppctl show memif on both
tap1/tap0 has no IP address vtysh -c "show running-config", then sv reload /services/frr
IP on the TAP, but not in VPP vppctl show lcp (lcp-sync on, the itf-pair exists)
testpmd fails to start R2 and R3 must create the vhost-user sockets (server) before testpmd starts. Check the hugepages (grep -i huge /proc/meminfo)
Memory regions (total 0) on VPP testpmd is not running or not connected: check the testpmd> terminal
BGP R2 ↔ R3 stays Active/Connect testpmd: show port info all (link up), show port stats all; VPP: show vhost-user
Route in FRR, but not in VPP vppctl show ip fib <prefix> (source lcp-rt-dynamic), ip route

Cleanup

Stop testpmd (quit at the testpmd> prompt), then:

containerlab destroy -t lab4.clab.yml

LAB 5 – VRRP + GoBGP & Bird

Goals

This lab is not about the Linux data plane. It is about tools that connect a Linux server to the network around it. Two web servers share one service IP (VIP). keepalived decides which server is active, and GoBGP advertises the VIP only from the active server. A BIRD route reflector rewrites the route attributes based on BGP communities. After this lab you should be able to:

  • use GoBGP as a BGP speaker on a server and advertise a prefix with large communities from the CLI,
  • use keepalived (VRRP + health check) to start actions (advertise / withdraw) when a server becomes master or backup,
  • configure BIRD as an iBGP route reflector, and read an advanced BIRD export filter that uses communities as "action" signals,
  • check the result in GoBGP, BIRD (birdc) and FRR (vtysh), and test a failover.

Topology

Addressing

Node Interface Address Software
www-1 eth1 10.1.0.2/30 (+ VIP when master) nginx, keepalived, GoBGP (AS 65001)
www-2 eth1 10.2.0.2/30 (+ VIP when master) nginx, keepalived, GoBGP (AS 65002)
R1 eth1 10.1.0.1/30 FRR (AS 64512)
eth2 10.2.0.1/30
eth3 10.10.0.1/24
lo 100.65.0.1/32
R2 eth1 10.10.0.2/24 FRR (AS 64512)
lo 100.65.0.2/32
bgp-rr eth1 10.10.0.3/24 BIRD 3 (AS 64512, route reflector)
lo 100.65.0.3/32

Service VIP: 100.64.1.100/32.

Management addresses (network 172.16.0.0/24): R1 .11, R2 .12, bgp-rr .13, www-1 .21, www-2 .22, l2-switch .40.

Control plane

  • OSPF area 0 between R1, R2 and bgp-rr (BIRD) on 10.10.0.0/24. It carries the loopbacks and the server subnets. R1's eth1/eth2 are passive in OSPF.
  • eBGP R1 (AS 64512) ↔ www-1 (AS 65001) and R1 ↔ www-2 (AS 65002). On R1 this is the peer group gobgp with remote-as external and passive: R1 never opens the BGP connection itself, and only accepts connections on TCP 179. GoBGP on the server opens the session after gobgp neighbor add.
  • iBGP AS 64512: R1 and R2 are route-reflector clients of BIRD (100.65.0.3). R1 sends all paths to the RR (addpath-tx-all-paths) and all communities (send-community all).
  • VRRP (keepalived) between www-1 and www-2, in unicast mode (unicast_peer). The servers are on different subnets, so multicast VRRP would not reach the other server.

What is already configured when the lab starts:

  • FRR on R1 and R2 (OSPF + BGP). The BGP sessions to the servers and to the RR are not up yet.
  • GoBGP on www-1 and www-2: only the global part (AS and router-id in /etc/gobgp/gobgp.toml), with no neighbors.
  • keepalived on www-1 and www-2, with the VRRP instance, the health check and the VIP. It has no notify actions yet. The config includes /etc/keepalived.d/*.conf inside the vrrp_instance, and this directory is empty.
  • BIRD on bgp-rr with OSPF, the kernel protocol and the export filter. It has no BGP sessions yet. The config includes /etc/bird.d/*.conf, and this directory is empty.

Your job is to:

  1. add the BGP neighbor to GoBGP on both servers,
  2. make keepalived advertise / withdraw the VIP through GoBGP,
  3. add the BGP route-reflector config to BIRD.

Deploying the lab and accessing nodes

Go to the lab directory, deploy the lab and list its nodes:

cd lab5
containerlab deploy -t lab5.clab.yml
containerlab inspect -t lab5.clab.yml

containerlab inspect lists six nodes in state running, with their management IP addresses.

To open a shell on a node:

docker exec -it www-1 sh         # www-1, www-2, bgp-rr, r1, r2

CLIs: gobgp (www-1, www-2), birdc (bgp-rr), vtysh (r1, r2).

Note: Do not run ./setup.sh or /tmp/setup.sh. Those scripts are the reference solution. In this lab you type every command yourself.

Task 0 – Check the starting point

0.1 OSPF [ optional ]

Check OSPF on R1 and on the route reflector (BIRD), and the routes that BIRD installed in the kernel:

docker exec -it r1 vtysh -c "show ip ospf neighbor"
docker exec -it bgp-rr birdc show protocols
docker exec -it bgp-rr birdc show ospf neighbors
docker exec -it bgp-rr ip route

Expected result: R1 has two OSPF neighbors on eth3, 100.65.0.2 and 100.65.0.3, in state Full. BIRD shows ospf_main ... Running. The kernel on bgp-rr has proto bird routes to 10.1.0.0/30, 10.2.0.0/30 and the loopbacks.

0.2 VRRP – the VIP is on www-1

Check which server has the VIP on eth1:

docker exec -it www-1 ip -br addr show eth1      # 10.1.0.2/30 100.64.1.100/32
docker exec -it www-2 ip -br addr show eth1      # 10.2.0.2/30 only

keepalived writes its log to the container output. Read it from the host with docker logs:

docker logs www-1 2>&1 | grep Keepalived_vrrp
docker logs www-2 2>&1 | grep Keepalived_vrrp

Expected result on www-1:

Keepalived_vrrp[66]: (lab5) Entering BACKUP STATE (init)
Keepalived_vrrp[66]: VRRP_Script(check_http) succeeded
Keepalived_vrrp[66]: (lab5) Changing effective priority from 110 to 130
Keepalived_vrrp[66]: (lab5) Entering MASTER STATE

On www-2 the effective priority changes from 100 to 120, and the instance stays in BACKUP STATE.

Use docker logs -f www-1 to follow the log live. This is useful during the failover test in Task 5.

How the priorities work:

  • Base priority: www-1 110, www-2 100.
  • The health check check_http runs curl http://127.0.0.1/ every 2 s, with weight 20. While the check succeeds, keepalived adds 20 to the priority: www-1 130, www-2 120.
  • If nginx on www-1 fails (fall 2 = two failed checks), its priority drops to 110. That is lower than 120, so www-2 becomes master.
  • When the check passes again (rise 2), www-1 is back at 130 and takes the VIP back (preemption).

0.3 BGP is not up yet [ optional ]

Check GoBGP on www-1, the BGP sessions on R1 and the BIRD include directory:

docker exec -it www-1 gobgp global
docker exec -it www-1 gobgp neighbor              # empty
docker exec -it r1 vtysh -c "show bgp summary"    # 10.1.0.2, 10.2.0.2, 100.65.0.3: Active or Connect
docker exec -it bgp-rr ls /etc/bird.d/            # empty

gobgp global shows AS: 65001 and Router-ID: 10.1.0.2. On R1 no session is established yet (Up/Down is never).

Task 1 – www-1: GoBGP neighbor and keepalived actions

Open a shell on www-1:

docker exec -it www-1 bash

1.1 Add the BGP neighbor (R1) to GoBGP

Add R1 as a BGP neighbor of GoBGP:

gobgp neighbor add 10.1.0.1 as 64512

Verify:

gobgp neighbor
gobgp neighbor 10.1.0.1

Expected result:

Peer        AS  Up/Down State       |#Received  Accepted
10.1.0.1 64512 00:00:04 Establ      |        0         0

  BGP state = SESSION_STATE_ESTABLISHED, up for 00:00:04
  Local address is 10.1.0.2, local ASN: 65001

This neighbor is added at run time through the GoBGP API. It is not saved to gobgp.toml, so it is lost if GoBGP restarts.

1.2 Add the notify actions to keepalived

keepalived runs a notify_master command when the instance becomes master, and a notify_backup command when it becomes backup. Use them to advertise or withdraw the VIP in GoBGP. The route gets two large communities. BIRD reads them as instructions (see Task 3.1):

  • 64512:1:777: set MED to 777
  • 64512:2:3: prepend the AS path 3 times
cat  > /etc/keepalived.d/notify.conf <<EOF

notify_master "/usr/local/bin/gobgp global rib add -a ipv4 100.64.1.100/32 large-community 64512:1:777,64512:2:3"
notify_backup "/usr/local/bin/gobgp global rib del 100.64.1.100/32 -a ipv4"
EOF

Restart keepalived so it reads the new file, and runs notify_master when it becomes master again:

sv restart /services/keepalived

Verify (wait a few seconds):

ip -br addr show eth1           # the VIP is on eth1 again
gobgp global rib

Expected result:

   Network              Next Hop             AS_PATH              Age        Attrs
*> 100.64.1.100/32      0.0.0.0                                   00:00:02   [{Origin: ?} {LargeCommunity: [ 64512:1:777, 64512:2:3]}]

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

1.3 Verify on R1

Check the BGP session to www-1 and the VIP route on R1:

docker exec -it r1 vtysh -c "show bgp summary"
docker exec -it r1 vtysh -c "show bgp ipv4 unicast 100.64.1.100/32"

Expected result: the session to 10.1.0.2 is up, with PfxRcd 1. For prefix:

  65001
    10.1.0.2 from 10.1.0.2 (10.1.0.2)
      Origin incomplete, valid, external, best (First path received)
      Large Community: 64512:1:777 64512:2:3

Task 2 – www-2: GoBGP neighbor and keepalived actions

Open a shell on www-2:

docker exec -it www-2 bash

www-2 uses the same commands, but its own neighbor address and different community values:

  • 64512:1:888: MED 888
  • 64512:2:1: prepend once

Add neighbor, keepalived scripts and restart keepalived:

gobgp neighbor add 10.2.0.1 as 64512

cat  > /etc/keepalived.d/notify.conf <<EOF

notify_master "/usr/local/bin/gobgp global rib add -a ipv4 100.64.1.100/32 large-community 64512:1:888,64512:2:1"
notify_backup "/usr/local/bin/gobgp global rib del 100.64.1.100/32 -a ipv4"
EOF

sv restart /services/keepalived

Verify:

gobgp neighbor                  # 10.2.0.1 64512 ... Establ
ip -br addr show eth1           # no VIP: www-2 is BACKUP
gobgp global rib

Expected result: www-2 is backup, so it does not advertise the VIP. Its RIB has only the route that R1 sends to it, which is www-1's route:

   Network              Next Hop             AS_PATH              Age        Attrs
*> 100.64.1.100/32      10.2.0.1             64512 65001          00:00:05   [{Origin: ?} {LargeCommunity: [ 64512:1:777, 64512:2:3]}]

Exit the remote shell using:

exit

On R1, both sessions to the servers are now up:

docker exec -it r1 vtysh -c "show bgp summary"

Task 3 – BIRD: route reflector with an advanced export filter

3.1 The existing BIRD config

First read the config that is already there:

docker exec -it bgp-rr cat /etc/bird/bird.conf

It has these parts:

router id 100.65.0.3;: the BIRD router ID.

protocol device: reads the interface list from the kernel every 5 s. Other protocols need it.

protocol ospf v2 ospf_main: OSPF area 0 on eth1 (broadcast) and lo (stub). import all takes all OSPF routes into the BIRD table master4. The export filter rejects BGP routes, so BGP is never redistributed into OSPF.

protocol kernel: writes routes from master4 into the Linux routing table. Only OSPF routes are exported (RTS_OSPF, RTS_OSPF_IA, RTS_OSPF_EXT1/2). BGP routes stay in BIRD only. The RR is not in the traffic path, so it does not need them in its kernel.

function prepend_times(int n): a reusable function with a parameter. It prepends the AS path up to 3 times. Each prepend uses a different (private) ASN, so you can see in the path how many prepends were done:

n Prepended (leftmost first)
1 64521
2 64522 64521
3 64523 64522 64521

filter export_to_clients: applied to every route the RR sends to its clients. lc c; declares a local variable of type large community. The filter runs these steps in order:

Step Code What it does
– if source != RTS_BGP then reject; Export only BGP routes. OSPF/device routes are never sent over BGP.
